content: 1. Gastrointestinal symptoms typically manifest within 4 to 10 days and are observed in 60–80% of cases. These include lower chest or epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, hiccups, diarrhea (sometimes with mucus), abdominal cramps or diffuse abdominal pain (occasionally localized to the right upper quadrant with liver tenderness), and conjunctival injection. Hypovolemia and dehydration, potentially leading to shock, may also occur. 2. After 10 days, complications may include hypovolemic shock, dehydration, neurological abnormalities, hemorrhagic manifestations, and late complications or recovery. Neurological symptoms may include confusion, disorientation, agitation (which may result in falls), bradypsychia (difficulty maintaining attention), extreme weakness (inability to stand or walk), and diminished consciousness or coma. Death can occur within 24–48 hours following the onset of neurological symptoms. 3. Hemorrhagic complications may present as gum bleeding, melena, hematemesis, epistaxis, or bleeding from puncture and IV line sites. 4. Recovery is marked by the resolution of gastrointestinal symptoms and fever, increased appetite, improved energy levels, and convalescent weakness. However, secondary infections (e.g., candidiasis, oral ulcers), multiorgan failure, tachypnea (Kussmaul breathing due to acidosis), seizures, and death may occur. Electrolyte abnormalities can also lead to complications in patients who initially had favorable outcomes. 5. Lassa fever has an incubation period of 6–21 days. Clinical differentiation among viral hemorrhagic fevers (VHFs) is challenging, necessitating prompt laboratory testing to confirm Lassa fever and initiate ribavirin treatment early. Swollen face and neck are classic signs of Lassa fever but occur in only 10% of cases and are absent in Ebola/Marburg infections. Sore throat is common in both, but exudative pharyngitis and convalescent hearing loss are more indicative of Lassa fever. Liver tenderness is more suggestive of Ebola/Marburg. 6. Approximately 20% of Lassa fever patients develop hemorrhagic symptoms. Lassa fever typically has a more indolent onset, with patients experiencing fatigue and feverishness for several days. In contrast, Ebola/Marburg infections have a more abrupt onset and rapid progression. In 80% of Lassa fever cases, the infection is mild or asymptomatic, with serologically diagnosed inapparent infections being common in endemic areas. The overall case fatality rate is low, but hospital studies report rates of 15–25%. Severe multisystem disease occurs in a subset of patients, with mortality rates as high as 80% in some epidemics. 7. Lassa fever is more severe during pregnancy, particularly in the third trimester, with frequent maternal mortality and 80% fetal loss. The virus is excreted in urine for 3–9 weeks and in semen for up to 3 months post-infection. The extent of sexual transmission remains unknown. 8. Severe Lassa fever progresses through clinical stages. During convalescence, transient alopecia and ataxia may occur. Sensorineural hearing loss (eighth cranial nerve) is common, affecting 29% of confirmed cases, with only half recovering some function. Laboratory findings include early lymphopenia followed by late neutrophilia, moderately depressed platelet counts, and abnormal platelet function. Elevated aspartate aminotransferase (AST) levels (>150) and high viremia are poor prognostic indicators. Albuminuria and hemoconcentration may accompany severe disease. 9. Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever (CCHF) has an incubation period of 3–7 days, depending on the mode of acquisition, with a maximum of 9 days after a tick bite and 13 days after contact with infected blood or tissues. CCHF presents with a wide spectrum of severity, from mild to fatal, with a case fatality rate of 5–30%. The onset is sudden, with symptoms such as headache, high fever, anorexia, lethargy, back pain, joint pain, abdominal pain, and vomiting. Jaundice and mood or sensory changes may occur in severe cases. 10. The hemorrhagic phase of CCHF is typically short (2–3 days, up to 2 weeks) and begins between days 3 and 5 of illness. Hemorrhagic manifestations range from petechiae to large hematomas on mucous membranes and skin. Common bleeding sites include the nose (epistaxis), gastrointestinal tract (hematemesis, melena, intra-abdominal bleeding), uterus (menorrhagia, other vaginal bleeding), urinary tract (hematuria), and respiratory tract (hemoptysis). Uncontrolled bleeding at injection sites and cerebral hemorrhage have been reported. Hepatosplenomegaly is observed in approximately 30% of patients. 11. Laboratory findings in CCHF include thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, elevated liver enzymes, and prolonged bleeding times. Laboratory values normalize within 5–9 days in survivors. Early clinical signs of CCHF are nonspecific and overlap with Ebola/Marburg and Lassa fever, making differentiation reliant on exposure history and laboratory testing. Poor prognostic indicators include age >60 years, rapid clinical and laboratory deterioration, somnolence, platelet count <50,000/mm³, or prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT). 12. Any acute febrile illness not attributable to a common pathogen or unresponsive to empirical therapy should raise suspicion for VHF, particularly if there is unexplained bleeding or rapid clinical deterioration. 13. Ebola screening involves a thorough interview and observation of symptoms, contact history, and local epidemiology. Physical exams are not performed in the screening area, but body temperature is checked. Health workers should wear light personal protective equipment (PPE) during interviews and full PPE when accompanying patients to isolation wards. Screening areas should maintain a 1–2 meter distance between screeners and patients, with physical barriers when possible. 14. Patients meeting suspect or probable Ebola case definitions should be isolated, counseled, and provided with oral rehydration solution (ORS). Physical exams and malaria rapid diagnostic tests are deferred to the ward. Suspect or probable cases should be reported to the surveillance system, and contact tracing should be initiated. 15. Pregnant or postpartum women meeting Ebola suspect or probable case definitions, or those presenting with Ebola-associated complications, must be managed as potentially infectious until proven negative by blood PCR testing. Full PPE and infection prevention and control (IPC) measures are required for their care. 16. Fever history within the last 48 hours is a valid indicator of fever, even if suppressed by antipyretics. Clinicians should observe for signs of illness, dehydration, or presyncope. Patients may deny symptoms to avoid admission to Ebola treatment units (ETUs). 17. For infants under 1 year, maternal history is crucial. If there is no Ebola history from the mother or family and no external contact, Ebola is unlikely. Screening should gather additional clinical and epidemiological information to determine admission as a suspect or probable case.
